newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers takes aim at federal "corporate welfare".
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers takes aim at federal "corporate welfare".

text.p: Charging that big business had been ripping off taxpayers far too long, a coalition of interest groups and key lawmakers Tuesday unveiled a 12-part hit list of "corporate welfare" programmes.

House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich, an Ohio Republican, is leading the unlikely coalition of liberal activists and conservative groups that wants to eliminate subsidies worth $11.5 billion over five years.

Programmes on the hit list include the Overseas Private Investment Corp., which provides loans and insurance to U.S. corporations that invest overseas; Forest Service road building; Agriculture Department rural electric cooperatives; the Animas La Plata public works project in Colorado and lawmaker-requested special highway construction projects.
"This is another step to end welfare as we know it," Kasich said. "This is just, just the beginning of what we intend to do. No one should think that we are satisfied."

Other targets include Energy Department programmes to reprocess plutonium and aid oil, coal and gas research; the Appalachian Regional Commission roads program; clean coal technology that the groups said business should pay for and some International Monetary Fund lending programmes.

Many of the programmes are familiar targets for budget cutters who have tried unsuccessfully for years to eliminate or reduce them. Kasich went after the Overseas Private Investment Corp. during the last session of Congress.
Lawmakers have also tried for years to end the Agriculture Department's Market Promotion Programme, another item on the list, which helps U.S. agribusiness promote products oveseas.

What was unusual about the news conference was the picture of consumer advocate Ralph Nader and environmental activists standing shoulder-to-shoulder with Kasich and conservative groups such as the National Taxpayers Union.
"There will be a lot of sparks flying as a result of this effort ... but it's going to be a refreshing battle royale here on Capitol Hill," Nader said.

Also Tuesday, a bipartisan group of senators including Republican John McCain of Arizona and Democrat Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts announced they will introduce a bill to set up an independent commision to review corporate welfare.

Kasich predicted the new coalition would provide the needed impetus to make the overdue reforms. While calling the coalition historic and comparing it to David battling Goliath, he and his allies carefully avoided taking on some giant business subsidies.

The hit list does not go after corporate tax breaks, which are under the purview of the powerful Ways and Means Committee. Kasich said he wanted to eliminate federal sugar subsidy and ethanol aid but they did not make the top 12.
"The failure will come if we don't stay focused ... if we keep talking about making the millions we won't make the first dollar," Kasich said.
Americans for Tax Reform, part of the coalition, said in a statement the group did not include tax breaks since "allowing taxpayers to keep more of their own money is not welfare."

Liberal activists made it clear they supported cuts in "corporate welfare" to free up more money for domestic spending. Conservative activists see cutting aid to business as one more step toward a balanced federal budget.
